what: Kernel #1 pass 3: measurement harness, and the cause of the 2x swing
answer: THROTTLING, not machine sharing. Claude was right.

harness.timing: CUDA events, never time.time around async launches
harness.gate: spread (p90-p10)/median <= 20% or the number is not publishable
harness.drift_control: same config measured at start and end of the session

clock_evidence.reading: The GPU spent the run at a median 585 MHz of 1590 boost and 30 W of an 80 W cap. That is a power-capped, low-occupancy state: the kernel is too small per launch to hold the clock up, so DVFS drops it, and every timing is measured at roughly a third of the clock the arithmetic assumes.

drift.reading: The same config drifted 2.4x between the start and end of one session, which is larger than any kernel change we have attempted. It explains the pass 1 vs pass 2 disagreement far better than the code did.

sweep.reading: 47 of 48 configurations could not be measured to within 20%. Only one config produced a stable number, and it happens to be the config the control used, which had the most warm-up.

implication.clock_headroom: At 1590 MHz instead of 585, the same work takes 2.72x less time: 1.1552 ms -> 0.425 ms, i.e. 20.7 -> 56.3 GB/s. So a large part of the apparent bandwidth failure is clock state, not kernel quality.
implication.but_not_an_excuse: Even at full boost 56 GB/s is 38% of the 150 target and 18% of peak, so the kernel is still not good enough. The throttling explains the 2x noise, it does not explain the gap to 150.

actions_for_pass_4: Every timed run must keep the sustained warm-up and must report SM MHz alongside GB/s.
Report sustained-clock figures as the honest T4 number, since that is what users get.
Clock locking was attempted; the result is recorded in 01_clocks.json and was not permitted on Kaggle.
Bigger tiles and more work per launch are now justified for a different reason than reuse: they keep the GPU busy long enough that DVFS does not downclock mid-measurement.

withdrawn.status: WITHDRAWN. That run had no warm-up and no clock logging, so it cannot be distinguished from a favourable clock sample.
PARTIALLY EXPLAINED. The measured drift of 139% within one session means most of that gap was clock state, not the uint32 change. The uint32 change is neither proven nor disproven.
